approved_card.ecological_causal_chain: Ending irrigation and cultivation stops the recurring conditions that favor crop species over dry-prairie vegetation. approved_card.ecological_outcome_if_protected: Over an expected establishment period of roughly ten to fifteen years, the restored belt becomes sufficiently wide and continuous to provide cover, feeding sites, and breeding habitat for movement-limited grassland insects and small reptiles. Should the regional planning commission choose habitat restoration that reconnects the prairie remnants or retain irrigated seed production to protect local economic stability?

approved_card.affected_people: Residents, fish-processing cooperatives, workshops, and ordinary shops in several remote settlements that depend on fuel delivered through the harbor for household heating and diesel-generated electricity.
approved_card.authority_check: The national government can implement either option because it owns the aggregate parcel, grants or withholds quarry rights, establishes coastal land-use restrictions, licenses the harbor works, and controls reconstruction funding and national fuel-reserve rules.
approved_card.balance_check: Authorization would cause persistent functional change across a productive marine inlet rather than a minor localized disturbance. Restriction would impose years of materially less affordable and less flexible heating and electricity across isolated communities rather than mere inconvenience. Ecological protections are not framed as preventing extinction, and human safeguards do not erase the recurring economic and energy-access burden.
approved_card.causal_plausibility_check: Tested Arctic breakwater designs commonly require large volumes of durable, graded aggregate. Excavation, crushing, runoff, and marine placement can deposit fines on kelp holdfasts and demersal spawning areas, while a larger breakwater can reduce circulation and increase sediment retention. Remote settlements with short shipping seasons plausibly incur higher costs and lower throughput when fuel is divided among small-barge voyages instead of full-size vessel deliveries.
approved_card.compromise_block: Engineering review finds that a shorter breakwater cannot satisfy the sea-ice, storm, and full-size-vessel safety standards, while any structure meeting those standards needs essentially the proposed aggregate volume. Inland deposits are ice-rich and fail structural tests. Other possible harbor locations are exposed to prevailing swells and would require a new road across thaw-sensitive ground, so they cannot safely serve full-size fuel vessels. Imported aggregate would require several seasons of bulk deliveries through the same restricted berth and weather window; those cargoes would displace enough fuel shipments to breach the guaranteed minimum heating reserve during reconstruction. Using fewer small barges remains possible only with the stated higher costs, allocation limits, and reliability burden, not as a way to preserve full energy service.
approved_card.culpability_check: Residents and businesses lawfully depend on the established fuel route for ordinary heating, electricity, and economic activity. Harbor operators did not cause the exceptional storm damage, and ecological protection is directed at prospective physical impacts rather than wrongdoing. Both interests are legitimate and described neutrally.
approved_card.decision_authority: The national government owns the raised beach, controls mineral extraction and coastal conservation designations, licenses harbors, and funds the proposed reconstruction. It can either prohibit industrial use of the parcel or authorize the quarry and harbor works.
approved_card.ecological_causal_chain: The land-use restriction prevents excavation, crushing, stockpiling, and haulage on the raised beach and leaves the enlarged breakwater without a technically suitable aggregate source. Avoiding those works prevents sediment runoff and marine-placement plumes, while avoiding the enlarged breakwater preserves the inlet's existing water exchange. Clearer substrate and continued circulation sustain kelp attachment, capelin spawning, benthic diversity, and the wider food web.
approved_card.ecological_outcome_if_not: Multi-year quarrying and marine placement release fine sediment that deposits on kelp holdfasts and capelin spawning substrate. The completed breakwater permanently narrows water exchange and increases retention of suspended material. Together these changes contract kelp and spawning habitat and shift the inlet toward a less diverse, silt-tolerant benthic community, reducing prey support for fish, seabirds, and seals.
approved_card.ecological_outcome_if_protected: The inlet remains in its present functioning condition: water exchange is not further restricted, quarry-derived sediment does not enter the shallows, and the connected kelp, spawning, benthic, seabird, fish, and seal relationships persist.
approved_card.ecologically_protective_option: Designate the raised beach as a no-quarry, no-industrial-use conservation zone, thereby preventing extraction of the aggregate required to reconstruct the harbor at its former full-size fuel-vessel capacity.
approved_card.human_causal_chain: The restriction removes the only tested local source with the required aggregate strength, grain distribution, and volume. The damaged harbor therefore remains limited to small barges. More voyages must fit within the same short weather window, increasing freight costs and capping annual fuel throughput; those constraints produce higher tariffs, fuel allocations, and scheduled interruption of nonessential commercial electricity use.
approved_card.human_outcome_if_not: The reconstructed harbor can again receive full-size seasonal fuel vessels, restoring predictable annual fuel inventories, lowering delivered energy costs, and avoiding routine allocation limits and scheduled commercial power cuts.
approved_card.human_outcome_if_protected: Fuel must be delivered through repeated small-barge shipments during a short calm-weather season. Transport costs substantially raise heating and electricity prices, while limited annual throughput requires household and business fuel allocations and occasional scheduled cuts to nonessential commercial power. National reserves and priority rules preserve minimum household heating and uninterrupted power for clinics, emergency services, and other essential facilities.
approved_card.human_protective_option: Authorize quarrying on the raised beach and use the aggregate to reconstruct the harbor with a breakwater and approach suitable for full-size seasonal fuel vessels.
approved_card.moderate_harm_check: The restriction causes prolonged high energy bills, constrained ordinary fuel use, and recurring business interruptions. The national government owns an adjacent raised beach containing the only aggregate tested as suitable and available in sufficient volume to rebuild the harbor for full-size seasonal fuel vessels. Heating and electricity prices would rise substantially, households and businesses would face fuel allocations, and nonessential commercial power would sometimes be cut. Minimum household heating and essential services would remain protected. Rebuilding the harbor would restore predictable fuel inventories, lower energy costs, and avoid routine limits. Should the national government choose the conservation zone that protects the marine ecosystem or authorize the quarry and harbor works that protect reliable energy access?

approved_card.affected_people: Owners of family-run date groves whose mature orchards are private property and whose lawful delivery contracts support the land’s established agricultural use, crop income, and market value.
approved_card.authority_check: The authority controls the relevant water right and all infrastructure that divides water between the springs and canal. Statute assigns it annual allocation responsibility, and the orchard contracts expressly permit reduced deliveries under shortage schedules. It can therefore implement either option without regulating land outside its jurisdiction or depending on another institution’s discretionary decision.
approved_card.balance_check: The ecological option maintains occupied habitat and connectivity across the entire range of a uniquely local species, while the human-protective option preserves a major portion of productive, capital-intensive private orchards and leaves the snail surviving in two channels. The comparison is neither species extinction versus a trivial cost nor severe human deprivation versus a marginal ecological gain.
approved_card.causal_plausibility_check: Multi-year instruments establish the relationship among bypass volume, channel depth, temperature, and dissolved oxygen, while population surveys confirm occupation and exchange among the four channels. Orchard irrigation and yield records establish peak summer demand and the effects of recurrent deficits on mature palms. The same measured dry-season water volume supplies both the ecological bypass and canal deliveries, so increasing one necessarily reduces the other.
approved_card.compromise_block: Monitoring shows that any bypass below 1.8 million litres per day still allows the two lowest channels to stagnate, and intermittent or nighttime-only releases fail because the channels warm and lose oxygen between releases. All groves already use maintained drip systems, so ordinary efficiency upgrades cannot recover the disputed volume. Nearby groundwater is too saline for sustained use on date palms, and the system has no unused dry-season storage. Alternating full-delivery years would expose the lower snail populations to lethal conditions in each agricultural-priority year; natural barriers prevent reliable recolonization. Replacing mature palms with less water-intensive crops would itself surrender the owners’ existing orchard use and require years before replacement plantings generated comparable income. Financial payments could offset some losses but would not preserve the mature orchards or their established use.
approved_card.culpability_check: Growers planted and maintained their orchards under valid contracts, use efficient irrigation, and have not caused the shortage through unauthorized pumping. approved_card.decision_authority: The public land-management authority holds the controlling groundwater and spring-flow rights, operates the wells, bypass gates, and canal headworks, and has statutory and contractual authority to allocate the available dry-season supply between spring bypass flow and reduced agricultural deliveries.
approved_card.ecological_causal_chain: The reserved bypass maintains adequate depth and continuous movement in all four channels. approved_card.ecological_outcome_if_not: The two lowest channels become warm, stagnant pools during the hottest weeks and lose their resident snail populations. If the dam is completely removed, twice-daily saline inundation and sediment exchange will restore salt-marsh vegetation, benthic invertebrates, juvenile-fish nursery use, and feeding access for larger fish and fish-eating birds, reestablishing a connected estuarine food web across the polder and adjacent bay.

Yet residents would permanently lose their current homes, historic village site, familiar landscape, and exact place-based relationships. Renewing and rehabilitating the dam would allow them to remain safely in their homes and preserve their daily-support networks, but the estuarine food web would not return. Gate schedules, a ring levee, and elevating homes cannot both protect present residence and substantially restore the food web. Should the environmental regulatory agency remove the dam to protect trophic integrity or renew it to protect residents’ continued residence?

approved_card.affected_people: Families from dispersed valley villages who hold a three-day annual vigil at the ancestral cemetery. The established practice combines collective grave cleaning, sung family histories, preparation and sharing of meals, and instruction of younger participants at the graves. The case does not rely on extinction, deaths, displacement, or trivial financial savings, so neither option is morally dominant by construction.

The excluded alternatives are tied to mapped terrain, road-safety requirements, portal and spoil footprints, and the defining elements of the vigil rather than to a generic assertion that compromise is impossible.

The only lower alignment lies in the mapped runout of the active landslide and cannot satisfy public-road safety standards. A tunnel is not an ecologically clean substitute: stable portal locations and the required spoil and equipment areas would occupy old-growth forest, while the unstable landslide-side geology precludes a portal outside it. approved_card.title: Cloud-forest access road and the annual graveside vigil

assignment.ecological_object_definition: A long-established ecosystem shaped by extended ecological continuity, with mature structure, species assemblages, and processes that are difficult to recreate quickly.
assignment.human_interest_definition: People's ability to continue an established social, cultural, or traditional practice that has meaningful importance to a community.
assignment.policy_mechanism_definition: Cancelling a planned infrastructure project, such as a road, pipeline, power facility, or development, because of its ecological effects.

final_dilemma:
A landslide has destroyed the only vehicle road to an ancestral cemetery and ceremonial clearing used by families from dispersed mountain villages. A narrow pedestrian path remains, but reaching the site requires about six hours of steep walking each way. The annual three-day vigil includes cleaning graves, singing family histories, sharing meals, and teaching younger participants at the graves. Many elders and residents with limited mobility can no longer attend, and those who can walk cannot carry the food, tools, and ceremonial materials needed for the full gathering. Without vehicle access, the vigil continues only in a smaller, age-selective form.

An intermunicipal public authority has approved a replacement road across the intact slope surrounding the cemetery. Construction would remove mature trees, old forest soils, roots, and deadwood from a centuries-old cloud forest. The permanent road opening would expose its edges to greater sunlight and wind, reduce humidity, eliminate epiphyte-bearing host trees, and divide continuous interior habitat for decades. Cancelling the road would retain the forest’s closed canopy, humid interior, mature structure, decomposer processes, and uninterrupted cover for forest-dependent animals, but would leave only the pedestrian path. Constructing it would restore practical vehicle access so people of varied ages and abilities could again carry out the complete graveside vigil.

Should the intermunicipal public authority cancel the replacement road to protect the old-growth cloud forest, or construct it to protect the community’s traditional graveside practice?

output.rationale: The draft faithfully preserves the assigned old-growth ecosystem, cultural practice, infrastructure-cancellation mechanism, and intermunicipal decision-maker. Both causal chains are plausible and licensed by the approved card, the cultural burden is meaningful but moderate, and the choice is concretely incompatible because cancelling the project leaves only the existing pedestrian path while construction creates a persistent vehicle corridor through the forest. Neither side is culpabilized or made trivially dominant. The draft is self-contained, neutrally framed, formatted as three short paragraphs, and ends with a direct decision question.

approved_card.affected_people: Community sailing students, adaptive paddling participants, instructors, and regular small-craft users who depend on the sheltered basin for recurring recreation. The reservoir’s other arms are exposed to stronger wind, wakes, and motor traffic and do not provide equivalent conditions for beginner instruction or assisted paddling.
approved_card.authority_check: The state natural-resources agency controls aquatic-pesticide permits and manages the state-owned reservoir and its recreation facilities. It can deny treatment and accept the resulting vegetation closure, or authorize and contract for the treatment needed to maintain the basin.
approved_card.balance_check: The ecological stake is the irreversible local loss of a documented, adaptively differentiated component of the pondweed population, rather than temporary damage to an ornamental plant bed. The human stake is the sustained loss of established sailing and adaptive-paddling opportunities, rather than inconvenience or reduced scenic quality. Neither side faces extinction, severe deprivation, or a merely trivial burden.
approved_card.causal_plausibility_check: Systemic aquatic herbicides can injure physiologically similar non-target plants occupying the same water and sediment. Repeated reproductive failure in a spatially restricted ecotype can remove associated alleles even when another ecotype survives. Hydrilla can rapidly regenerate from tubers and viable fragments, and dense mats can obstruct launches and small-craft maneuvering. Site-specific genetic surveys and multi-year control trials support each critical link.
approved_card.compromise_block: Three years of agency trials found that spot treatment left enough connected hydrilla to restore obstructive mats before peak recreation season, while expanding treatment to the effective dose exposed nearly all warm-shoal pondweed because its stems are interwoven with hydrilla. Cutting and harvesting produced viable fragments and did not deplete the sediment tuber bank; bottom barriers buried both species. The reservoir’s other arms exceed the programs’ established wind, wake, and motor-traffic limits, and no other agency reservoir within routine day-trip distance has a comparably sheltered accessible launch. These facts exclude a lower-dose, mechanical, spatial, or on-site relocation compromise under the present decision.
approved_card.culpability_check: The recreational programs lawfully use an authorized public facility and did not introduce hydrilla. The native pondweed is a non-target species. The conflict arises from biological intermingling and the limits of available control methods, not misconduct by either affected side.
approved_card.decision_authority: The state natural-resources agency owns and manages the reservoir, issues aquatic-pesticide treatment permits, and can approve or prohibit systemic-herbicide use in the sheltered basin. approved_card.ecological_outcome_if_not: Repeated treatment eliminates most flowering warm-shoal plants and sharply reduces their recruitment. approved_card.ecological_outcome_if_protected: The warm-shoal and deep-water pondweed ecotypes retain viable breeding stands across the depth gradient. Their differentiated alleles and continuing gene exchange preserve the reservoir population’s range of heat- and depth-associated traits.
approved_card.ecologically_protective_option: Prohibit systemic aquatic-herbicide treatment within the sheltered basin, preventing repeated non-target exposure of the native pondweed ecotypes.

assignment.decision_maker: a state or provincial natural-resources agency
assignment.ecological_object_definition: Variation in genes within a species or population, which preserves distinct lineages and the range of biological traits they contain.
assignment.human_interest_definition: People's ability to continue meaningful leisure activities or access recreational spaces they regularly use.
assignment.policy_mechanism_definition: Restricting or prohibiting the use of pesticides or similar chemicals in order to reduce ecological harm.

final_dilemma:
A state natural-resources agency must decide whether to permit annual basin-wide systemic herbicide treatment in a state-owned reservoir’s only sheltered sailing and paddling basin. Dense hydrilla mats have spread through the launch lanes, instruction circuit, and assisted capsize-recovery area, making them unusable. Treatment at the concentration and duration supported by agency trials would suppress hydrilla enough to keep the basin navigable for sailing instruction, adaptive paddling, recovery practice, and regular small-craft recreation. The reservoir’s other arms have stronger wind, wakes, and motor traffic and cannot provide equivalent conditions; without treatment, hydrilla will again cover the usable basin within two growing seasons, ending these programs and regular use of the sheltered water.

Yet hydrilla is interwoven with native pondweed that includes distinct warm-shoal and deep-water ecotypes. Several heat- and depth-associated alleles are concentrated in the warm-shoal plants. Repeated systemic-herbicide exposure would eliminate most flowering warm-shoal plants and sharply reduce their recruitment. Although deep-water pondweed would remain, the reservoir would lose the ecotype holding most of its warm-shoal and heat-associated alleles. Prohibiting treatment would preserve viable breeding stands across the depth gradient, along with their differentiated alleles and continuing gene exchange. Agency trials and site constraints have ruled out lower-dose, mechanical, spatial, and relocation alternatives that would avoid these consequences.

Should the agency prohibit systemic herbicide treatment to protect the pondweed’s genetic diversity, or authorize it to protect established sailing and adaptive-paddling recreation?

output.rationale: The draft faithfully preserves the assigned ecological object, recreational interest, pesticide-regulation mechanism, and agency decision-maker. Its causal claims are licensed by the approved card, including the concentration of heat-associated alleles in the warm-shoal ecotype and the role of both trials and site constraints in excluding compromises. The options are concretely incompatible, the recreational harm is moderate but meaningful, neither side is culpabilized, and the three-paragraph format ends with a direct decision question.

approved_card.affected_people: Island residents, including tradespeople, apprentices, shift workers, families, and small businesses that regularly travel or transport vehicles between the island and mainland.
approved_card.authority_check: The regional government controls the project sponsor, capital authorization, construction contracts, and seabed works approval. It can lawfully cancel the fixed link before construction and continue allocating operating subsidies to the ferry service.
approved_card.balance_check: The ecological stake is the lasting fragmentation of an extensive tidal nursery system through altered flow, sedimentation, and loss of continuous shallow habitat. The human stake is a major improvement in routine mobility for an entire island population, not merely recreational convenience. Conversely, cancellation preserves connectivity without imposing isolation, forced relocation, or loss of essential access, so neither option is trivially dominant.
approved_card.causal_plausibility_check: Site-specific tidal-volume measurements, hydraulic modelling, sediment-flume tests, eelgrass mapping, and fish and invertebrate surveys support the predicted scour, deposition, and loss of habitat continuity. Geotechnical borings, navigation-clearance rules, surveyed approach grades, and the mapped village footprint support the limits on bridge redesign. Ferry logs document fares, queues, capacity limits, timetable gaps, and weather-related reductions.
approved_card.compromise_block: Adding several culverts would not preserve broad tidal exchange: hydraulic modelling shows that discrete openings would still concentrate flow and leave depositional zones behind the embankments. A fully elevated bridge would require navigation clearance over the marked channel and long approach grades, but the island approach reaches the existing village before the necessary grade could return to ground level. Lowering the bridge would obstruct the navigation channel. The deep soft-sediment basin also requires closely spaced foundations, so a nominally open viaduct would still disturb eelgrass and redirect shallow flow. Avoiding both the village footprint and the nursery beds would require a different landing corridor outside the approved project, not a local redesign. Ferry subsidies can reduce monetary burdens but cannot provide unrestricted overnight or spontaneous vehicle travel.
approved_card.culpability_check: Island residents are pursuing ordinary travel, employment, education, family, and commercial needs; they did not create the geographic barrier or the fixed link's hydraulic effects. The ecological interests arise from existing habitat use and physical tidal processes. Neither side is described as blameworthy.
approved_card.decision_authority: The regional government sponsors and funds the fixed-link project, controls the regional road agency, holds the seabed works authorization for the approved corridor, and has final authority to cancel construction while continuing ferry support.
approved_card.ecological_causal_chain: Solid approach embankments occupy most of the naturally broad, shallow tidal cross-section. The remaining navigation span cannot pass the same tidal volume without concentrating velocity near the opening and reducing circulation elsewhere. Concentrated flow scours eelgrass at the span, while low-energy areas trap sediment and narrow tidal creeks. Those changes remove the linked shallow habitats through which juvenile fish and invertebrates move between nursery areas and the outer bay.
approved_card.ecological_outcome_if_not: The solid embankments close most of the sound's cross-section. Flow accelerates through the short bridge opening, scouring the adjacent eelgrass, while reduced circulation behind the causeways causes fine-sediment accumulation and contraction of tidal channels. The resulting scour and deposition break the continuous shallow-water route between the outer bay, eelgrass beds, and tidal-creek nurseries used by juvenile fish and dispersing invertebrates.
approved_card.ecological_outcome_if_protected: Twice-daily tidal exchange remains distributed across the full width of the shallow sound. Water, suspended sediment, fish, larvae, and dispersing invertebrates continue moving among the outer bay, eelgrass beds, and tidal-creek nurseries, preserving the sound as a connected habitat system.
approved_card.ecologically_protective_option: Cancel the fixed link and maintain the subsidized year-round passenger-and-vehicle ferry under its existing service pattern.
approved_card.human_causal_chain: Cancellation leaves the tidal crossing dependent on ferries. Boarding, loading, and unloading add time to each trip; scheduled sailings create waits; vehicle deck capacity requires booking at busy times; fares increase trip costs; and the overnight gap prevents spontaneous travel. Subsidies can reduce fares and secure service continuity but cannot make vessel travel continuous or eliminate loading and weather constraints.
approved_card.human_outcome_if_not: Residents gain predictable direct travel at any hour, without ferry fares or vehicle-space reservations. Mainland jobs, classes, services, family visits, and commercial deliveries become faster and easier to reach, particularly for people with irregular schedules or vehicle-dependent work.
approved_card.human_outcome_if_protected: Islanders retain safe, year-round mainland access, including vehicle transport, but remain subject to fares, advance planning, loading queues, finite vehicle space, sailing intervals, an overnight service gap, and occasional weather-related timetable reductions. These constraints continue to burden irregular shifts, evening education, family visits, shopping, and spontaneous trips.
approved_card.human_protective_option: Build the causeway-and-bridge link, allowing direct road, bus, bicycle, and pedestrian travel without ferry fares, loading queues, sailing intervals, vehicle-capacity limits, or overnight timetable gaps.
approved_card.moderate_harm_check: Cancellation does not strand residents or deny access to necessities: the ferry is safe, subsidized, year-round, and carries both passengers and vehicles. The harm remains meaningful because recurring waits, fares, booking constraints, limited late service, and reduced spontaneity affect employment, education, family life, commerce, and social participation across the island.

final_dilemma:
A regional government must decide whether to cancel a planned causeway-and-bridge link between a populated island and the mainland. Most of the crossing would be solid embankment, leaving only a short bridge over the navigation channel. If built, the embankments would close most of the shallow sound’s tidal cross-section. Flow would scour eelgrass near the bridge and reduced circulation would deposit sediment behind the causeways, narrowing tidal channels. The continuous shallow-water route linking the outer bay, eelgrass beds, and tidal-creek nurseries would be broken, disrupting movement by juvenile fish and dispersing invertebrates.

Cancelling the project would preserve tidal exchange across the sound and maintain this connected habitat system. Islanders would still have safe, subsidized, year-round ferry access for passengers and vehicles, but would continue to face fares, queues, advance booking during busy periods, sailing intervals, limited vehicle space, an overnight service gap, and occasional weather-related reductions. These constraints affect shift workers, apprentices, families, tradespeople, and businesses making regular mainland trips.

Building the link would allow direct road, bus, bicycle, and pedestrian travel at any hour, without ferry fares, loading delays, reservations, or timetable gaps. Should the regional government cancel the fixed link to protect habitat connectivity, or build it to protect islanders’ mobility?

approved_card.affected_people: Aquaculture crews, net-maintenance contractors, boat operators, fish-processing workers, and local businesses that depend on the community-owned farm’s regular payroll, production schedule, contracts, and purchases.
approved_card.authority_check: Delegated marine legislation gives the elected council binding authority over chemical-discharge permits and aquaculture operating conditions throughout the tenure. The council can deny the pesticide permit, impose harvest and fallowing conditions, inspect compliance, or authorize discharge; neither the operator nor a regional agency can override its decision within this lagoon.
approved_card.balance_check: One option prevents the extinction of a species confined to a single lagoon. The other preserves a major source of predictable employment, contracting, processing activity, and business revenue in a remote community. The human interest is ordinary economic continuity rather than luxury or marginal profit, while the ecological interest is supported by a direct non-target toxicity mechanism rather than speculative ecosystem claims.
approved_card.causal_plausibility_check: Crustacean-targeting aquaculture bath pesticides can kill non-target crustaceans after discharge. Whole-habitat exposure is credible in a shallow lagoon with weak exchange when occupied eelgrass beds surround the treatment area. Mandatory early harvest and fallowing plausibly reduce harvest weight, annual output, processing throughput, and marine-service work in a community whose businesses depend on regular production schedules.
approved_card.compromise_block: Timing treatment outside amphipod breeding periods is inadequate because multiple amphipod life stages remain in the eelgrass throughout the year and recurring lice outbreaks do not occur on a controllable seasonal schedule. Treating fewer pens still releases enough pesticide into the weakly flushed lagoon to reach all occupied beds. Onboard filtration trials have not reduced dissolved pesticide to the amphipod-safe concentration. Exporting spent treatment water by well-boat is not feasible because the nearest licensed receiving facility lies beyond the safe operating range of available vessels. Moving the pens outside the lagoon is unavailable because the council’s marine tenure ends at the lagoon boundary and the exposed offshore site exceeds the certified limits of the existing mooring system.
approved_card.culpability_check: The community-owned farm and its workers conduct licensed aquaculture and comply with fish-health requirements. The sea-lice outbreaks, the pesticide’s non-target effects, and the amphipod’s narrow geographic range are not deliberate harms caused by either workers or conservation advocates. Both sides seek legitimate protection of community interests.
approved_card.decision_authority: The elected Indigenous governing council holds delegated final authority over chemical-discharge permits and aquaculture operating conditions within the community’s marine tenure. It can either authorize the pesticide discharge or prohibit it and enforce alternative operating conditions.
approved_card.ecological_causal_chain: The bath pesticide is formulated to kill crustacean sea lice and is also toxic to non-target crustaceans. Tarpaulins enclose the treatment only during dosing; afterward, the spent water must be released. Weak lagoon exchange retains the dissolved pesticide, and tidal mixing carries it from the pens into all occupied eelgrass beds. Repeated exposure kills breeding adults and juveniles before population recovery can occur. Because the amphipod exists only in this lagoon, no external source population can recolonize the beds.
approved_card.ecological_outcome_if_not: Spent treatment water disperses through every occupied eelgrass bed during recurring treatment cycles. Adult and juvenile amphipods are killed faster than the population can reproduce, and the absence of any population outside the lagoon prevents recolonization, resulting in extinction of the endemic species.
approved_card.ecological_outcome_if_protected: The endemic amphipod avoids pesticide exposure at lethal and reproduction-impairing concentrations and continues reproducing throughout the lagoon’s eelgrass beds, preserving a species found nowhere else.
approved_card.ecologically_protective_option: Deny permits for use and discharge of the crustacean-targeting bath pesticide in the lagoon. When lice exceed the mandatory fish-health threshold, require affected pens to be harvested early, emptied, and fallowed rather than chemically treated.
approved_card.human_causal_chain: If chemical treatment is prohibited, binding fish-health rules require pens exceeding the lice threshold to be harvested early and then fallowed. Fish sold below planned harvest weight generate less revenue, and idle periods reduce total output. Irregular harvest volumes shorten processing runs and reduce hours for farm crews, processors, boat operators, net contractors, and maintenance workers. Lower payroll and contracting expenditures then destabilize other businesses in the remote community.
approved_card.human_outcome_if_not: The farm retains regular production and harvest cycles, sustaining predictable aquaculture payrolls, processing shifts, vessel and maintenance contracts, and routine purchasing from local businesses.
approved_card.human_outcome_if_protected: Recurring early harvests and mandatory fallowing reduce harvest weight, interrupt processing schedules, and leave pens idle. The resulting production decline causes rotating layoffs, fewer processing shifts, loss of vessel and maintenance contracts, and unstable revenues for community businesses. Community income guarantees and utility protections prevent homelessness, hunger, or loss of essential services, but do not restore dependable work or commercial activity.
approved_card.human_protective_option: Authorize in-pen tarpaulin bath treatments and the subsequent permitted release of spent treatment water into the lagoon, allowing stocked fish to remain in production through their planned harvest cycle.
approved_card.moderate_harm_check: The prohibition causes persistent employment disruption, reduced working hours, contracting losses, and instability in the community’s commercial base. These are substantial local economic harms, but income guarantees, housing support, and utility protections keep them below severe deprivation, forced relocation, or danger to health and safety.

final_dilemma:
A remote Indigenous coastal community operates salmon pens in a shallow lagoon under its marine tenure. Eelgrass beds around the pens are home to an amphipod found nowhere else. When recurring sea-lice outbreaks exceed mandatory fish-health thresholds, the elected Indigenous governing council must decide whether to permit a crustacean-targeting bath pesticide. Although tarpaulins contain the treatment during dosing, the spent water must then be released. In the weakly flushed lagoon, it disperses into every occupied eelgrass bed, killing adult and juvenile amphipods faster than they can reproduce. Repeated treatments would drive the lagoon’s endemic species to extinction.

If the council denies the permits, affected pens must be harvested early, emptied, and fallowed. Lower harvest weights and idle periods reduce production, interrupt processing schedules, and cause rotating layoffs, fewer shifts, and lost vessel and maintenance contracts. Local businesses lose predictable purchases and revenue. Income guarantees and housing and utility protections prevent homelessness, hunger, and loss of essential services, but they do not restore dependable work or commercial activity. Authorizing pesticide discharge would preserve regular harvest cycles, payrolls, processing work, contracts, and business activity, while extinguishing the amphipod.

Should the elected Indigenous governing council choose to deny pesticide permits and protect the endemic species, or authorize discharge to protect local economic stability?
